seo.title: Karmic tail 6 8 20 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 8 20 compatibility in the destiny matrix: The Lovers, Justice and Judgement, a couple whose love takes in the other's family from day one.

title: Karmic tail 6-8-20 in compatibility: “thy people shall be my people”
short: The words “whither thou goest, I will go… thy people shall be my people” have been read at weddings for generations. They were not spoken by a bride to her groom. A young widow said them to her mother-in-law. That shift holds the whole secret of the karmic tail 6-8-20 in destiny matrix compatibility: this couple's love takes in the other's family from the very first word, the road to a shared life runs through honest measure and open agreement, and the main task is kin: a family that raises people up instead of judging them.

sections.h2: A book that opens with the word “judges”
paragraphs: The Book of Ruth is one of the shortest books in the Bible: four chapters, 85 verses. In Christian Bibles it comes straight after the Book of Judges, and it opens: “Now it came to pass in the days when the judges ruled.” The Hebrew is denser still, “in the days of the judging of the judges”: the word for judgement appears twice in the very first line.

The plot fits into a paragraph. In a famine, Elimelech of Bethlehem takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to the country of Moab. He dies there; the sons marry two Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and about ten years later they die too. Naomi sets off for home. Orpah says goodbye to her on the road; Ruth stays and makes her vow. In Bethlehem the barley harvest is beginning, and Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz, a kinsman of her late father-in-law. On her mother-in-law's advice she goes to him at night on the threshing floor. In the morning Boaz sits down at the city gate, calls ten elders and settles the matter, before witnesses, with a kinsman who is closer by blood. Then he marries Ruth. Their son Obed is the grandfather of King David.

The book's three main scenes are the three cards of the tail, in the same order. The vow on the road is The Lovers, the entry and the shared wish. The field, the measure of barley and the hearing at the gate are Justice, the road. The last page, where the name of the dead is raised up and the family tree is written out, is Judgement, the main task. Even the atmosphere matches: the first five verses are a journey into a foreign land and three deaths, and the centre of the chart of such couples almost always holds The Fool or Death.

The roles in the story are not tied to gender. Either partner can be the “stranger” in a family, and the plot is not about a woman and a man. It is about how two people enter each other's family line.

sections.h2: The Lovers at the entry: a vow that already includes the mother-in-law
paragraphs: Here is the vow in full: “Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God: where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried” (Ruth 1:16–17).

The entry to the task in a couple's tail is what the two want together: shared wishes, agreements, a “common language”. For a 6-8-20 couple that language sounds like Ruth's vow: **I want not only you, I want your world.** One sentence holds a people, a faith, a home and even a grave. The end of the tail is already written into its beginning: to be buried in the ground of another family is to enter that family. The Lovers here are not a spark but a decision to follow.

Waite calls The Lovers “the card of human love, here exhibited as part of the way, the truth and the life”, and in a very high sense “a mystery of the Covenant”. Ruth's vow is exactly that, a covenant, and it is about a road: it does not answer the question “what do I feel?”, it answers “where will I go?”.

In the book whose vow is read at weddings, **the word “love” appears exactly once**: in the last chapter, where the women of Bethlehem speak to Naomi of “thy daughter in law, which loveth thee” (4:15). Ruth and Boaz never speak of love to each other. Another word does the work instead: hesed, a loyalty that does more than it owes. The King James Bible renders it as “kindness”. Naomi wishes her daughters-in-law well for the way they “have dealt with the dead, and with me” (1:8), and Boaz tells Ruth: “thou hast shewed more kindness in the latter end than at the beginning” (3:10).

There is one more clue, and English readers can see it for themselves. The formula of marriage in Genesis reads: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife” (Gen 2:24). Both of its verbs stand in the Book of Ruth. Boaz says to Ruth: “thou hast left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity” (2:11). And of the parting on the road the text says: “but Ruth clave unto her” (1:14), the same Hebrew verb as in Genesis, which the King James Bible keeps as clave and cleave. The marriage formula is fulfilled long before the wedding, and it is addressed to a mother-in-law. That is what the entry of the 6-8-20 tail looks like: from the first step, love binds not two people but two people together with their families.

Beside Ruth stands the other daughter-in-law. Orpah weeps, kisses her mother-in-law and goes “back unto her people, and unto her gods” (1:15). The book does not condemn her: Orpah acts sensibly, and Naomi herself lets her go. The Lovers at the entry are a choice with a lawful alternative. A couple with this tail takes the hard road not because there is no other.

In everyday life it shows in small things. From the first winter one of the two spends the holidays with the other's relatives, and a year later calls them “ours”. The couple chooses where to live by asking which of the parents will soon need help. “We're one family” means, for this couple, literally one family for everyone.

The entry point sits on the line of tasks, so the wish can turn into resistance. “Your people are my people” easily becomes “my people are gone”. Ruth left her father, her mother and her homeland, and a couple can repeat that step too literally: living for years with one partner's parents, depending on them for money, dissolving its own way of life into someone else's. Among Lisovskaya's tasks for The Lovers in a couple there is this dependence on relatives, the insecurity that breeds jealousy and control, and an idealised picture of the union, the wish for a family that is “the way it should be”. Sometimes two people meet after a hard past, as Ruth and Naomi did after three deaths in the family, and then the entry is a shared wish to trust people again.

sections.h2: Justice in the middle: a field whose edge the law leaves uncut
paragraphs: The middle of the task is how the couple travels from the shared wish to the main task. For Ruth that road is not a romance but work. The second and third chapters are taken up with a field, a measure and a right.

Ruth goes out to glean, and that is not charity but law. Leviticus commands: “thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest… thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger” (Lev 19:9–10). The justice of this tail begins with the edge of a field left uncut on purpose for a stranger. In a 6-8-20 couple that edge is room for the other: for their relatives, habits and past, which are not reaped to suit oneself.

Boaz goes further than the law. He tells his young men: “Let her glean even among the sheaves, and reproach her not: and let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her” (2:15–16). The stalks are dropped deliberately, so that she has something to find and does not feel indebted. This is justice gentler than the letter, but it does not cancel the letter: Ruth still works until evening.

In the evening she beats out what she has gathered, “and it was about an ephah of barley” (2:17). The ephah is the very measure Leviticus speaks of: “Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have” (19:36). A chapter later a measure restores the balance of a whole family. Back home, Naomi had said of herself: “I went out full, and the Lord hath brought me home again empty” (1:21). Boaz measures out six measures of barley for Ruth and says: “Go not empty unto thy mother in law” (3:17). In Hebrew it is one word, reikam, “empty”. Justice in the middle of the tail works like scales: something went out, something has to come back, and the couple keeps count so that nobody is left empty. The Talmud reads the six measures as a hint at six famous descendants of Ruth (Sanhedrin 93b): the measure of barley is already counting a family line.

A midrash explains why the book was written at all: “This scroll contains nothing of purity or impurity, of what is forbidden or permitted. Why, then, was it written? To teach how great is the reward of those who do kindness” (Ruth Rabbah 2:14; our translation). Kindness and reward, hesed and recompense: The Lovers and Justice in one sentence. The book lays down no laws of its own; it shows how laws already given can be kept with kindness.

The scene has a counterpart in the sky. Waite writes that the female figure on the Justice card “is said to be Astræa”. In his poem Phaenomena (third century BC) Aratus describes her constellation: “the Maiden, who in her hands bears the gleaming Ear of Corn”; men called her Justice, and once she lived among them, “assembling the elders, it might be in the market-place or in the wide-wayed streets”, and “ever urging on them judgements kinder to the people” (translated by G. R. Mair). **An ear of corn in her hand and the elders in the market-place**: in the Book of Ruth these are the field and the city gate. Justice here is not a sword but a measure of grain and a judgement that is kind to people.

Keats, in “Ode to a Nightingale” (1819), saw Ruth differently: “sick for home, / She stood in tears amid the alien corn”. The Bible has no tears in the field. People weep on the road, at the parting; in the field they work, eat bread with the reapers and carry home an ephah. That is the exact difference between the minus and the plus of the middle: a 6-8-20 couple can live for years with a sense of the “alien field” and a quiet grievance, or it can keep count: what it brought, what it received, what the other is short of.

Measure has a second side, equal weight. Boaz enters the book as “a mighty man of wealth” (2:1), and he calls Ruth “a virtuous woman” (3:11). In Hebrew it is one word, hayil, strength and worth: gibbor hayil and eshet hayil. The rich owner of the field and the poor foreign widow weigh the same on these scales. The Justice of a 6-8-20 couple at its best is like that: income, age and origin do not make one of the two a debtor.

Then the matter moves to the gate, the place where an ancient town held its courts. Boaz could have settled it all at night on the threshing floor, but he says: “there is a kinsman nearer than I” (3:12). In the morning he sits at the gate, calls ten elders and lays out the case in front of everyone. Another man's right outweighs his own wish, and Boaz risks losing Ruth in order to win her honestly. An ancient gesture seals the deal: “a man plucked off his shoe, and gave it to his neighbour: and this was a testimony in Israel” (4:7), and even the narrator explains it as a custom of “former time”. Twice the key words of Justice ring out: “Ye are witnesses this day” (4:9–10).

The scene also holds the minus of the middle, a man without a name. In Hebrew Boaz hails him as peloni almoni, “so-and-so”; the King James Bible keeps it as “Ho, such a one!”, while the Russian Synodal translation drops the address altogether. Such-a-one is glad to take the field: “I will redeem it.” But when he hears that with the field he must marry the widow, “to raise up the name of the dead”, he backs out: “I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance” (4:5–6). This is Justice that measures everything by itself: the gain, yes; the obligation, no. Deuteronomy called the man who refused “The house of him that hath his shoe loosed” (25:10). In the Book of Ruth he takes off his shoe himself, yet he gets no name of any kind: **the man who would not keep another's name alive has no name of his own in the story.**

Every 6-8-20 couple has its own such-a-one. Not a third person but an inner calculation that now and then speaks in one partner's voice: “I can't, it would mar my inheritance.” My holiday, my money, my weekends with my parents. The accounts are honest in themselves; the trouble begins when they are kept in silence.

At its best such a couple takes a long look before deciding, and wants to formalise the relationship not for the stamp: for these two, an agreement is a form of respect. Duties are shared fairly, big purchases are discussed in advance, and the family always has a plan B. At its worst the ledger is kept in the head: who went to whose parents for New Year, who put how much into the repairs at the in-laws', whose promise has been broken again. One partner takes everything on, “I'll talk to your mother myself”, and a year later that responsibility has turned into control over every phone call. The other withdraws whenever something goes wrong in the family. The two start living like neighbours under contract. Among Lisovskaya's tasks of Justice in a couple the core is put briefly: owning one's share of the blame instead of accusing everyone around, and learning to forgive.

The numbers confirm the picture of the scales. The middle of this tail is the exact sum of its ends: 6 + 20 = 26 → 8. Justice literally holds two pans, The Lovers on one and Judgement on the other, love and kin. And in one couple in eight (12%) the same structure appears at the level of the two people: one partner has The Lovers in the middle of their personal tail, the other has Judgement. One brings love into the union, the other brings kin, and they meet in Justice.

sections.h2: Judgement as the main task: the kinsman who raises up a name
paragraphs: The main task is the couple's chief trial, and it is read mostly through what does not work. In Lisovskaya's book the key to the twentieth energy in a couple is kin and family: relatives, traditions, inheritance, the parents' influence on the two. Waite calls the card The Last Judgment, the resurrection of the dead, and its inner meaning is the great work of transformation in answer to a summons. Wen opens Judgement with spiritual awakening and epiphany, and adds: “It is about salvation.” The Book of Ruth joins these readings in a single phrase.

At the gate Boaz explains what it is all for: “to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance” (4:5) and “that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren” (4:10). Deuteronomy uses the same language: a brother-in-law who will not marry his brother's widow “refuseth to raise up unto his brother a name in Israel” (25:7). **Judgement is the card of the dead rising. In the Book of Ruth it is the name of the dead that rises, and it is raised not by angels but by relatives.**

The key word of the book is go'el. It appears more than twenty times. The King James Bible renders it as “kinsman” (“one of our next kinsmen”, 2:20; “thou art a near kinsman”, 3:9), and the verb at the gate as “redeem”. A go'el is the relative bound to buy back the land of a brother who has fallen into poverty (Lev 25:25); in the Book of Ruth a second duty is woven into the first, to keep the name of the dead from dying out. The same word stands in Job, in a verse that Christian tradition has read for centuries as a promise of resurrection: “For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth” (Job 19:25). The “redeemer” there is the same go'el. In translation the link is half hidden: “kinsman” in one book, “Redeemer” in the other. In Hebrew it is one word, and in both verses it sits beside the verb “to rise, to raise”: to raise up the name of the dead in Ruth, to stand up upon the dust in Job. Handel set Job's verse at the opening of Part Three of Messiah: I know that my Redeemer liveth.

This is the secret of the 6-8-20 main task. **In this tail “kin” and “redeemer” are one word.** A family can be a court: it sizes up the stranger, decides for the two of them and passes sentence. Or it can be a go'el: it buys back, brings home and raises up. The couple's task is to move both their families from the first meaning to the second.

The book is honest about the minus, too. The union of Ruth and Boaz is planned by the mother-in-law: “My daughter, shall I not seek rest for thee?” (3:1). Naomi herself chooses the kinsman, the night and even what her daughter-in-law should wear. Among the tasks of Judgement, Lisovskaya names exactly this: relationships built on the parents' approval or arranged through relatives. In a modern couple it is the introduction “through Mum”, the wedding where the elders decided everything, the flat bought by one side's parents, which comes with a say in everything along with the square metres.

The second task in the same list is a love hindered by age, position and tradition. Boaz is older: he blesses Ruth “inasmuch as thou followedst not young men” (3:10). Ruth is a Moabite, and Deuteronomy says: “An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord; even to their tenth generation” (23:3). The dispute over origins outlived the couple itself. In the Talmud (Yevamot 76b–77a) the standing of David, Ruth's great-grandson, is challenged because of his great-grandmother, and the dispute is settled by a reading: a Moabite, but not a Moabitess. Relatives can sit in judgement on a stranger for a very long time. In a 6-8-20 couple it shows in phrases like “that's not how they do things” and “what do you expect from a family like that”.

The third is a partner who decides nothing without the parents. Ruth answers her mother-in-law: “All that thou sayest unto me I will do” (3:5). Obedience in itself is no disaster yet. The disaster is when no voice of one's own remains behind it.

The fourth is boundaries that are either missing or built like a wall. In the last chapter it is Naomi who holds the child of Ruth and Boaz: “And Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it.” And the boy is named by the neighbours: “And the women her neighbours gave it a name, saying, There is a son born to Naomi” (4:16–17). For an ancient book this is a happy ending. For a modern couple it is a familiar scene: the child is named after someone because “that's been decided”, the holidays follow one side's timetable, and in the new family the voice of the two sounds quieter than anyone's.

In Waite's list for Judgement reversed the first words are “weakness, pusillanimity”. In this story pusillanimity has a name, such-a-one: he hears that the name of the dead must be raised up, and he does not rise. The minus of the main task is not malice but this “I can't”: I can't tell my mother, I can't go against my father, I can't admit I was wrong. Lisovskaya says the same plainly: unwillingness to own one's mistakes, and a relationship in which neither partner can say what they feel or what they dislike.

sections.h2: A night on the threshing floor: where the couple finds its own voice
paragraphs: The turning point is the third chapter. Naomi gives Ruth detailed instructions and ends them with: “and he will tell thee what thou shalt do” (3:4). Ruth agrees: “All that thou sayest unto me I will do.” And she does it, until midnight. At midnight Boaz wakes and asks: “Who art thou?” Ruth speaks first, and not what she was told: “I am Ruth thine handmaid: spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman” (3:9). The words “you are a go'el” are her own: Naomi never mentioned redemption.

Boaz answers with the very phrase Ruth had just given her mother-in-law. In Hebrew the two lines are almost word for word the same, “all that you say, I will do”; the King James Bible blurs it into “I will do to thee all that thou requirest” (3:11). The chain has turned around: the younger woman obeyed the older one, and now the owner of the field does what the foreigner said. The family's plan is carried out, but the voice in it is now her own. **That is the strong version of Judgement in a couple's tail: the two neither fight the family nor dissolve in it; they take the family's design and speak their own word inside it.**

Her sentence holds one more detail. The Hebrew for “skirt” is kanaf, which means both a wing and the hem of a garment. Boaz used the same word when he blessed Ruth in the field: “The Lord recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the Lord God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust” (2:12). The King James Bible hides the echo, “wings” in one place and “skirt” in the other. Ruth asks Boaz to become the answer to his own blessing. He wished her a reward for her deeds, and turned out to be that reward himself. This is how the middle of the tail passes into the main task: the justice one wishes on another has to be carried out oneself.

The place, too, is no accident for a reader of the Bible. A threshing floor is where grain is winnowed: the threshed crop is tossed into the air and the wind carries off the chaff. In the Bible it is an image of judgement. The first psalm: the ungodly “are like the chaff which the wind driveth away. Therefore the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment” (Ps 1:4–5). John the Baptist says of the one who is coming: “Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt 3:12). And Boaz “winnoweth barley to night in the threshingfloor” (Ruth 3:2). The couple's decisive night takes place where grain is parted from chaff. For the 6-8-20 tail it is an exact picture of the main task: to see what in the inheritance of two families is grain worth bringing into one's own home, and what is chaff that can be let go on the wind.

In the morning Boaz neither hides the night nor drags things out. Naomi tells Ruth: “Sit still, my daughter, until thou know how the matter will fall: for the man will not be in rest, until he have finished the thing this day” (3:18). Justice at its best is the speed of an honest decision: no stockpiling of things left unsaid, but out to the gate the same day.

At the gate the elders bless the marriage and name the foremothers: “like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel” and “let thy house be like the house of Pharez, whom Tamar bare unto Judah” (4:11–12). Tamar's name is a clue too. Her story (Genesis, chapter 38) is another story of a widow and of a kinsman who failed in his duty. When Judah was told that his daughter-in-law was pregnant, he passed sentence: “Bring her forth, and let her be burnt.” When he learned the truth, he said: “She hath been more righteous than I” (Gen 38:24–26). The ten-name genealogy that closes the Book of Ruth begins with Pharez, a child born of a trial in which the judge admitted his own guilt. In Lisovskaya's book the tasks of Justice and Judgement in a couple meet in one point, owning one's mistakes. The Book of Ruth lays that point at the foundation of a family line.

And the last to rise in the book is not one of the dead but a living woman. On her return Naomi asked: “Call me not Naomi, call me Mara” (1:20), that is, “bitter”. Nobody does: the name Mara never appears in the book again. At the end the women of Bethlehem tell Naomi that her grandson shall be “a restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age”. The Hebrew says “one who brings back the soul”, from the same verb Naomi used when she complained that the Lord had “brought me home again empty”. **Judgement in this couple is not a sentence but a return: whoever left empty comes back full.**

sections.h2: The centre and values of a 6-8-20 couple: a road, three deaths and a harvest
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's chart is its atmosphere, what lies between the two when nobody is watching. For couples with the 6-8-20 tail the centre is almost always one of two cards: 22, The Fool (50.2%), or 13, Death (47.2%); another 2.6% have 4, The Emperor. No other centre occurs, and that is arithmetic. In a personal matrix the entry of the tail is the sum of the main task and the centre, and for this couple the formula works by itself: 20 + 22 = 42 → 6, 20 + 13 = 33 → 6, 20 + 4 = 24 → 6. The middle, too, equals the sum of the ends. The couple's 6-8-20 tail is built like the tail of a single person, although two people add it up.

The first five verses of the Book of Ruth are exactly these two centres. The road: a family leaves for a foreign land, not knowing what awaits it there. Death: first the husband dies, and about ten years later both sons. In Lisovskaya's book The Fool at the centre of a couple is an atmosphere of freedom and trust, where the experience of past relationships has been taken into account and a difference in age or status does not get in the way; for Waite The Fool is “the spirit in search of experience”. Death at the centre is not a prediction of loss but a union that accepts the partner's past and moves on; in the minus, traits of former partners are projected onto the present one. Both of the usual centres speak about the past: a 6-8-20 couple lives alongside what came before it, earlier families, losses, another life. The question is whether that past pulls the couple back or becomes experience.

“The couple's values” are what the union exists for. For these couples it is 3, The Empress (50.1%), 21, The World (27.8%), or 12, The Hanged Man (22.1%). What follows is our reading, not a statement from the books. Waite's divinatory list for The Empress opens with the word “Fruitfulness”, and in his description he calls her “the door or gate by which an entrance is obtained into this life”; Lisovskaya's key to the Three is fertility and growth. The Book of Ruth is a book of harvest, from “the beginning of barley harvest” to the end of the wheat harvest. The World in Waite's list reads “recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place”: a value for a couple in which someone has come from far away. The Hanged Man is the value of waiting: “Sit still, my daughter, until thou know how the matter will fall.” Waite ends his description of The Hanged Man with a sentence that contains both the centre and the main task of this couple: “after the sacred Mystery of Death there is a glorious Mystery of Resurrection”.

sections.h2: How the 6-8-20 tail adds up: an example with two dates
paragraphs: A couple's tail is not calculated from the sum of the dates. First each partner's personal matrix is built, then the matching points of the two matrices are added and the sum is reduced to 22. The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: it, too, is the sum of the personal middles.

An example: 05.12.1975 and 14.08.1975. The first partner's main task is 12 (5 + 12 + 22 = 39 → 12), the centre is 6, the personal tail is 18-3-12. The second partner's main task is 8 (14 + 8 + 22 = 44 → 8), the centre is 7, the personal tail is 15-5-8. The points of the couple's tail:

This couple's centre is 13 (6 + 7), and “The couple's values” are 12. And every card of the tail appears in their chart twice. Judgement stands in the main task and in the point “What to create together”, the answer to the question of why the two met. Justice stands in the middle and in “Home and things”. The Lovers stand at the entry and in “What you teach” (the sphere “The couple as parents”). A repeat does not double a card, but it shows where else its theme is heard: a union that exists to create a family line runs its home by justice and teaches its children what it began with itself. And in every 6-8-20 couple The Lovers also stand in the “Common language” of the relationship line: it is the same point as the entry to the task.

In all, the 6-8-20 tail is made up of nine combinations of personal tails. The most frequent are 18-9-9 + 6-17-11 (25% of such couples), 15-5-8 + 18-3-12 (24%, as in the example) and 21-4-10 + 21-4-10 (23%). The last combination accounts for almost a quarter of all such couples: **the two have the very same personal tail, and together they produce a third that neither of them has.** Two Worlds give The Lovers (21 + 21 = 42 → 6), two Emperors give Justice, two Wheels of Fortune give Judgement.

The partners rarely bring these three cards with them. By our count over every date since 1900, in 38% of couples neither partner has 6, 8 or 20 anywhere in their personal tail. Judgement appears in one partner's personal tail in only 12% of couples, and always in the middle, and the other partner then has The Lovers in the middle. In 88% of couples neither partner brings the main task: kin becomes a task only when these two are together.

The tail occurs in roughly one couple in 32 (3.17%), eighth out of the 97 couple tails. No other order of these three numbers occurs among couple tails. A personal tail 6-8-20 does exist (1,141 dates since 1900), but it is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and it has an article of its own.

The tail does not promise an ending like Ruth's, nor does it threaten the opposite. It shows where this couple's work lies: in family, one's own and the other's. The book and the three cards yield a few points to lean on.

ul: **Say “ours” about both families, and decide as two.** Ruth carried out her mother-in-law's plan and spoke her own word inside it. Relatives can propose; what the couple does is decided by the two.
**Keep the accounts out loud.** This couple's justice lives at the gate, before witnesses, not in the head. A grievance in a secret ledger grows; one that is talked through is closed the same day.
**Leave the edge of the field.** Do not reap the other to suit yourself: their relatives, habits and past do not need remaking.
**Know your own such-a-one by sight.** When the voice inside says “I can't, it would mar my inheritance”, ask whether it is honest reckoning or pusillanimity.
**Own your share.** “She hath been more righteous than I”: the family tree that closes the book begins with that sentence.

**Raise up rather than judge.** Remember the dead and each other's earlier lives, do not erase names from the family's story; part the grain from the chaff instead of throwing out the whole inheritance.

**Don't let the neighbours name what is shared.** The child's name, the home, the holidays and the traditions of the new family belong to the two, even when the elders are right about everything else.

paragraphs: At its strongest, a 6-8-20 couple resembles the end of the book: two people from different families, with a gap in age and position, do everything openly, by measure and before witnesses, and their union gives life back to those who stood beside them.

ul: The Book of Ruth: the Russian Synodal translation; the Masoretic Hebrew text; the King James Bible (1611).

**6 · The Lovers: entry to the task.** What the couple wants together: a union in which “yours” becomes “ours”, the other's relatives, habits and past included. The same wish can turn into resistance when “ours” dissolves “mine”.

**8 · Justice: middle of the task.** How the couple moves towards the goal: by measure, by agreement, before witnesses, with no secret deals. The risk is to keep love on a ledger and guard “my own inheritance”.

**20 · Judgement: main task.** Kin and family: to accept the other's relatives without handing them the right to decide for the two of you, to own one's mistakes, to raise up what has died or fallen silent in both families.

intro: The tail turns up in roughly one couple in 32. The story in which these three cards stand in exactly this order was written down more than two thousand years ago, and it fits on a few pages.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-8-20 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a tail of the couple's matrix: The Lovers at the entry to the task, Justice in the middle and Judgement in the main task. The couple enters the union wanting “yours” to become “ours”, the other's family included, travels the road through honest measure and open agreements, and its main task is kin: to accept both families without giving them the right to decide for the two, and to own one's mistakes.

faq.q: Is this a difficult tail for a couple?
faq.a: The tail passes no sentence and predicts no events. It shows in which area the couple's main work lies: its relationship with family. At their best these three cards make a union in which relatives accept the partner, agreements are fair, and a difference in age or origin is no obstacle. At their worst they bring a ledger of grievances, the elders' decisions in place of the couple's, and silence about what matters.

faq.q: Will a couple with the 6-8-20 tail necessarily have trouble with relatives?
faq.a: No. Judgement in the main task points to a theme, not to a conflict. For some couples it is a theme of acceptance: entering someone else's family and becoming one of its own. For others it is a theme of boundaries: keeping the couple's voice alive beside strong elders. For others still the task is about memory: each partner's past, losses and earlier families.

faq.q: How is the couple tail 6-8-20 different from the personal tail 6-8-20?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date of birth, and its points mean something else. A couple's tail is added up from two personal matrices: each of its points is the sum of the matching points of two people. It is read as the task of the union: the entry is the couple's shared wish, the middle is its road, the main task is what the two have to learn together.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether it has the 6-8-20 tail?
faq.a: Two dates of birth are needed. A personal matrix is built for each, then the matching points are added: entry to entry, middle to middle, main task to main task, with each sum reduced to 22. The compatibility calculator does this by itself and shows the couple's tail together with the centre and the other points.

report: The vow “whither thou goest, I will go… thy people shall be my people” has been read at weddings for generations. It was not spoken by a bride to her groom: a young widow, Ruth, said it to her mother-in-law. The Book of Ruth has four chapters, and its three main scenes stand in exactly the order of the 6-8-20 tail: the vow on the road, the field and the hearing at the city gate, the family tree at the end.

report.h3: A love that takes in another family from the first word

report: The Lovers at the entry are what the couple wants together. For a couple with this tail the shared wish sounds like Ruth's vow: **not only the other person, but the other's whole world**, a people, a home, a faith and even a grave. In the book whose vow is read at weddings, the word “love” appears exactly once, and it is the love of a daughter-in-law for her mother-in-law. There is a subtler clue as well. The marriage formula of Genesis, “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife”, is fulfilled in the Book of Ruth in full. Boaz tells Ruth: “thou hast left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity”, and on the road “Ruth clave unto her”, with the very same Hebrew verb. The marriage formula is turned towards the other's family long before any wedding.

The same point can become resistance. “Thy people shall be my people” easily turns into “my people are gone”: years in one partner's parents' home, dependence on them, a way of life of one's own dissolved in someone else's.

report.h3: Justice that leaves the edge of the field

report: The middle of the tail is the road, and for Ruth it is not a romance but work. She gleans under a law that forbids reaping the corners of a field and leaves them “for the poor and stranger”. Boaz, the owner of the field, goes further than the law: handfuls are dropped for her on purpose. Measure restores the balance here. Naomi came home “empty”, and Boaz sends Ruth back to her with six measures of barley: “Go not empty unto thy mother in law.”

The minus of the middle has a name in the book, such-a-one: that is how Boaz hails, without a name, the kinsman who is closer by blood. The man is glad to take the field, but when he hears that the widow comes with it, he backs out: “I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance.” **The man who would not keep another's name alive has no name of his own in the story.** Every 6-8-20 couple has its own such-a-one: not a third person but an inner calculation, my time off, my money, my holidays with my parents. The accounts stay honest while they are kept out loud. When they are kept in silence, the two start living like neighbours under contract, remembering who went to whose parents and whose promise has been broken again.

The main task is Judgement, and the key to this energy in a couple is kin and family. At the gate in the Book of Ruth the question is how “to raise up the name of the dead”. The key word of the book is go'el, which the King James Bible renders as “kinsman”. The same word stands in Job: “For I know that my redeemer liveth.” **In this tail “kin” and “redeemer” are one word.** A family can be a court: it sizes up the stranger and decides for the two. Or it can buy back, bring home and raise up. The couple's task is to move both families from the first meaning to the second.

The price shows in the book itself. The union is planned by the mother-in-law: she chooses the kinsman, the night and even what her daughter-in-law should wear. At the end Naomi holds the child, and the neighbours name him, saying: “There is a son born to Naomi.” For an ancient book this is a happy ending. For a modern couple it is a familiar scene: the elders' decisions in place of the couple's, holidays on one side's timetable, and the voice of the new family quieter than anyone's. In Waite, Judgement reversed opens with the words “weakness, pusillanimity”. The minus here is not malice but “I can't”: I can't tell my mother, I can't admit I was wrong.

report.h3: The night the couple finds its own voice

report: The turn comes on the threshing floor. Naomi said: “he will tell thee what thou shalt do”, and Ruth promised: “All that thou sayest unto me I will do.” But at midnight she speaks first, and off script: “spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman.” Boaz answers with her own words, which in Hebrew repeat her promise almost exactly: “I will do to thee all that thou requirest.” **The family's plan is carried out, but the voice in it is now her own.** This is the strong version of Judgement: neither fighting the family nor dissolving in it, but speaking one's own word inside the family's design. Even the “skirt” is no accident: in Hebrew it is kanaf, a wing, the same word Boaz used when he blessed Ruth in the field, “under whose wings thou art come to trust”. The justice one wishes on another has to be carried out oneself.

A threshing floor is where grain is winnowed and the wind carries off the chaff, and in the Bible it is an image of judgement. The main task of a 6-8-20 couple is to see what in the inheritance of two families is grain worth bringing into one's own home, and what is chaff. And to own one's share: the family tree that closes the book begins with Pharez, son of Tamar, of whom Judah the judge said: “She hath been more righteous than I.”

On her return Naomi asked to be called Mara, “bitter”, and nobody ever called her that. At the end the women of Bethlehem tell her that her grandson will be the nourisher of her old age, in Hebrew “one who brings back the soul”. **Judgement in this couple is not a sentence but a return: whoever left empty comes back full.**
